journal_name: International Journal of Cooperative Information Systems

abstracts.abstract: The proliferation of decentralized data sources in cooperative information systems has exposed fundamental limitations in traditional interoperability frameworks, which predominantly rely on centralized mediation and rigid schema mappings. This paper presents a paradigm-shifting theoretical framework termed Dynamic Semantic Interoperability (DSI), which reconceptualizes how heterogeneous distributed information systems achieve alignment without requiring shared ontologies or centralized coordinators. Drawing upon coalitional game theory and distributed constraint satisfaction, DSI establishes formal conditions under which autonomous agents can progressively converge toward mutual understanding through localized semantic negotiations. We prove that DSI achieves global interoperability when agents follow bounded rationality strategies, provided the semantic overlap network exhibits specific structural properties. The framework's core innovation lies in replacing static interoperability mappings with emergent coordination protocols that adapt dynamically to evolving collaboration contexts. Our theoretical analysis demonstrates that DSI reduces communication complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) for n participating systems while maintaining semantic consistency guarantees. This work opens new theoretical directions for collaborative systems research by shifting the interoperability problem from architectural design to behavioral emergence. The proposed paradigm has significant implications for multi-agent systems, peer-to-peer information systems, and large-scale collaborative data management in open environments.

Business process management in distributed environments faces critical challenges in ensuring consistency when concurrent workflow modifications occur across organizational boundaries. This paper presents an enhanced theoretical model for distributed workflow consistency that significantly extends the classical Soundness property to multi-party cooperative settings. Our approach introduces Semantic Soundness with Distributed Agreement (SSDA), which formalizes correctness criteria accounting for autonomy constraints, temporal dependencies, and data integrity requirements inherent in collaborative systems. We develop a novel verification algorithm that reduces computational complexity from exponential to polynomial time for workflows exhibiting tree-structured control flow, representing a substantial improvement over existing approaches. The theoretical analysis establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for SSDA compliance, enabling early inconsistency detection during workflow design. Furthermore, we provide a compositional framework allowing workflow modules developed by different organizations to be verified independently before integration. Experimental evaluation on synthetic and real-world workflow specifications demonstrates that our approach achieves 94% reduction in verification time compared to state-of-the-art model checking techniques while maintaining equivalent diagnostic precision. This work advances the theoretical foundations of service-oriented computing by providing rigorous foundations for trustworthy inter-organizational process coordination.

Existing collaborative data management systems assume persistent connectivity and centralized coordination, rendering them inadequate for the increasingly prevalent edge computing and mobile collaboration scenarios. This paper introduces CollabMesh, a novel distributed information system architecture that fundamentally reconceptualizes collaborative work by treating intermittent connectivity as a first-class design principle rather than a failure condition. CollabMesh employs a hierarchical gossip protocol that enables intentional information sharing through opportunistic encounters, eliminating reliance on continuous network topology. The system architecture introduces Context-Aware Conflict Resolution (CACR), which utilizes provenance metadata and collaborative annotations to semantically merge conflicting operations without requiring centralized arbitration. We implemented CollabMesh as a middleware framework supporting multiple application domains, with specific instantiations for collaborative document editing and distributed sensor data aggregation. Extensive evaluation across emulated and real-world mobile networks involving 500+ participants demonstrates that CollabMesh achieves eventual consistency within bounded time despite 73% average network partitioning. User studies reveal that the system supports natural computer-supported cooperative work patterns while hiding infrastructure complexity from end users. The architectural paradigm enables cooperative information systems deployment in challenged environments including disaster response, vehicular networks, and remote field operations where traditional distributed systems fail.

Data integration in multi-agent cooperative information systems remains challenging when participating agents employ heterogeneous data models and autonomous schema evolution occurs frequently. This paper presents SmartIntegrator+, an enhanced data integration framework that substantially improves upon existing approaches through adaptive schema matching driven by machine learning and collaborative feedback mechanisms. Unlike prior systems relying on static mappings or heavyweight ontology alignment, SmartIntegrator+ continuously learns from integration outcomes and user corrections to refine its matching strategies. The system architecture incorporates a novel Peer-Mediated Reconciliation protocol that enables efficient resolution of semantic conflicts through localized negotiations, reducing coordination overhead compared to centralized mediation approaches. We deployed SmartIntegrator+ in a federated research data management scenario involving 12 autonomous institutions with distinct data standards. Quantitative evaluation shows 41% improvement in matching precision and 67% reduction in manual curation effort compared to traditional rule-based integration systems. The framework demonstrates robust performance under schema evolution, maintaining integration quality even when participating systems modify their data structures by 30% or more. This work provides a practical solution for collaborative data management in open multi-agent environments while preserving system autonomy and enabling incremental interoperability improvements.
